s.apropos.2: “I’m Still Mine” is a volunteer initiative that started in Lorient. It will be run by a non-profit association (under the French law of 1901), currently being set up, bringing together clinicians and volunteers.
s.apropos.4: No commercial activity. No advertising, no affiliate links, no paid partnership with any platform.
s.apropos.5: As little data as possible. No account, no tracking cookies, no audience measurement. The walkthrough runs entirely in your browser; we only receive what you choose to send (an image to check, an appointment request), and our server does not keep it.
s.apropos.6: No judgement. We do not tell anyone what to do. We give accurate information and an open door.
s.apropos.7: Content reviewed by clinicians. Every screen is approved by the medical committee before it is published.

s.plateformes.11: “I’m Still Mine” is a free, anonymous, non-judgemental 10-minute walkthrough for people considering adult content creation: leaks and permanence, real earnings, life afterwards, and a check for coercion. It is run by a non-profit with volunteer clinicians. We ask only for a plain link on your creator sign-up or safety page. No data is exchanged and no tracking is involved. English and other languages are planned.

s.photos.1: Check whether your photos are circulating
s.photos.2: Free tools already exist to stop your intimate images from being shared and to search for where a photo of you appears. Here they are, and in what order to use them.
s.photos.3: For your own photos only. Searching for someone else's images without their consent, even an ex's or a partner's, is an invasion of their privacy.
s.photos.5: You choose your intimate photos or videos on your phone. The site calculates a digital fingerprint of them on your device: the image itself never leaves your phone. Only the fingerprint is sent to partner platforms, which block or remove copies.
s.photos.6: Partner platforms include Facebook, Instagram, Threads, TikTok, Snapchat, Reddit, OnlyFans, Bumble, Bluesky and Aylo (Pornhub).
s.photos.8: For adults only. For an image taken before you turned 18: Take It Down.
s.photos.9: 2. Search for where a photo appears
s.photos.10: A reverse image search finds pages that contain the same photo, or a very similar one. Try several tools: they do not find the same results.
s.photos.11: Google LensThe broadest. Also works from the Google app. Bing Visual SearchOften gives different results from Google. TinEyeFinds exact copies, even cropped ones. Yandex ImagesOften effective with faces.
s.photos.12: Use a photo you posted yourself, then a version cropped to your face.
s.photos.13: These tools do not see everything: private groups, messaging apps and some websites are out of their reach.
s.photos.14: 3. If you find a leak or a deepfake
s.photos.15: Keep evidence first: the page address, the date, screenshots. Do not contact the person who posted it.
s.photos.16: Report it to the website. On Reddit, the report form has an option for intimate images posted without consent: reddit.com/report.
s.photos.17: Ask Google to remove the results: its help centre has a form for non-consensual explicit images, including fake ones.
s.photos.18: Report it to the authorities at internet-signalement.gouv.fr (Pharos), and file a complaint. In France, sharing a sexual deepfake without consent has been a criminal offence since the law of 21 May 2024.
s.photos.19: Don't face this alone: 3018 (online violence), 3919 (Violences Femmes Info, 24/7), or an appointment request in the walkthrough.
s.photos.21: Check an image you have found
s.photos.22: Compare a suspect image with your face after a live selfie, and look for signs of manipulation. Your selfie never leaves your phone; only the suspect image is checked by our server, then deleted.
s.outils.2: Your selfie and the face comparison stay on your device. Only the suspect image is sent to our server, in pieces, to look for manipulation: it is never stored and is released from memory as soon as we answer. Results are clues, not proof.
s.outils.7: You will be asked to turn your head in a random order. This prevents anyone from using someone else's photo: this tool is only for checking your own images.
s.outils.12: A screenshot is enough. If several people appear, each face is compared.
s.outils.14: Look for signs of generation or editing
s.outils.15: The image is sent to our server in shuffled pieces. It reads the file's hidden information: “AI-generated” labels, settings left by image generators, and face-editing apps. It gives a simple verdict, then deletes everything. It does not analyse the pixels yet: an image without any marker can still be a deepfake.
s.outils.17: For a clearer result, use the original file rather than a screenshot whenever possible.
s.outils.19: No tool knows your body better than you do. For each point, say whether the image is different from you. The differences are added to the report.
s.outils.20: You do not have to prove an image is fake to report it: sharing it without your consent is already an offence.
s.outils.22: To attach to a report or a complaint. Also keep the original file without changing it.
s.outils.23: Address of the page where you found it
s.confidentialite.2: The walkthrough collects nothing. Your answers stay in your browser and disappear when you close the tab.
s.confidentialite.3: No account, no tracking cookies, no audience measurement.
s.confidentialite.4: No connection logs. To prevent abuse, the server counts checks per IP address for one day. The address is replaced by a fingerprint computed with a key kept only in memory and changed every day: this is pseudonymisation, not perfect anonymity. The counter is deleted the next day.
s.confidentialite.5: What can be sent, and only if you choose to: the suspect image to check (never stored, released as soon as the verdict is given); your email address if you ask for a link to continue (deleted as soon as the link is sent); an appointment request (passed on by email to a volunteer clinician or to our coordination, with no copy on our server).
s.confidentialite.6: The “Quick exit” button replaces the page with a neutral website. Also remember to clear your history if someone has access to your phone.
s.confidentialite.7: Demo: this text must be legally reviewed (GDPR) before going live.

p.0.body:
Before you start, take ten minutes for yourself.

Maybe you are thinking about selling adult content online. Here, nobody judges you and nobody is trying to change your mind. We simply lay out what many people find out too late.

  • No account, no name, no email address.
  • Nothing is saved: closing the tab erases everything.
  • You can stop at any time, or skip a step.
The “Quick exit” button, at the bottom of every page, instantly replaces the screen with a neutral website.
p.0.minor:
These platforms are forbidden to minors, and anyone pushing you towards them is committing an offence.
In France, you can talk for free and anonymously to 119 (Allô Enfance en Danger) or 0 800 235 236 (Fil Santé Jeunes), 7 days a week. Elsewhere, call your country's emergency services (112 in the European Union).
p.1.body:
A published photo can never be fully taken back.

  • Leaks. Some websites copy and repost paid content, often within a few days. They shut down and reappear under other names.
  • Screen captures. A subscriber can record their screen. No platform can stop them.
  • Facial recognition. Public tools can find a face from a single photo, including on a professional or family profile.
  • Deepfakes. Your images can be used to make content you never made.
There are remedies (removal requests, reports, complaints), but they take time and never remove everything. The tools to check and block your images are on the Check my photos page.
p.1.q: If someone close to you came across these images in five years, how would you feel?
p.2.intro:
Advertised earnings are not real earnings.

Most accounts earn little: a few highly visible creators take most of the money. “Agencies” that promise thousands of euros should set off alarm bells.
p.2.label: What you imagine earning per month (gross)
p.2.perMonth: per month, before your own costs (equipment, clothes, time spent).
p.2.note: Rough estimate for France: 20% platform commission, social contributions of about 25% under the French micro-business scheme, plus income tax. If an agency also takes a cut, that comes on top. Check on urssaf.fr for your situation; in another country, taxes and contributions are different.
p.3.body:
Think about the person you will be in ten years.

  • Work. Some jobs and employers run thorough background searches: civil service, teaching, healthcare, security.
  • Family. Parents, a future partner, children: what is found online can resurface at the worst moment.
  • Safety. Persistent subscribers sometimes try to find out where you live. One detail in the background can be enough.
  • Wellbeing. The messages, the ever more extreme requests and the constant comparison are exhausting.
p.3.q: Is there a plan (studies, career, family) that this could make harder for you?
p.4.intro:
Is it really your decision?

Answer just for yourself. Nobody will see these answers.
p.4.c1: Is someone pushing you to start, or insisting?
p.4.c2: Does someone other than you have or ask for your passwords?
p.4.c3: Does someone take, or would someone take, part of the money without you really choosing it?
p.4.c4: Do you owe money to someone who is offering you this “work”?
p.4.c5: Do you feel you have to do it to have somewhere to live or food to eat?
p.4.alert:
What you describe may be coercive control or pimping, which is a criminal offence. It is not your fault.
In France: free, anonymous helpline on 3919 (Violences Femmes Info, 24/7); emergency 17 or text 114; support: Amicale du Nid (amicaledunid.org). Elsewhere: your country's emergency services (112 in the European Union). The “Talk to someone” step also lets you request an appointment.
p.5.intro:
Let's take stock, just for you.

Put each slider where you feel you are today.

p.5.s2: How comfortable you are with the idea of being recognised

o.tab3: 3. Did it come from my phone?
o.p.title: Find your camera's fingerprint (PRNU)
o.p.intro:
Every camera sensor has tiny flaws, invisible to the eye, that leave a kind of fingerprint in all its photos. If a suspicious image carries your phone's fingerprint, it is a real photo taken with your phone (a leak, not a generated image). If it doesn't, that proves nothing.

  • Choose 5 to 20 original photos taken with the same phone, straight from your gallery: no screenshots, no photos sent through WhatsApp or a social network, no filters.
  • Photos of the sky, light-coloured walls or bright landscapes give the best fingerprint.
  • The suspicious image must be exactly the same size as your photos. Images downloaded again from Reddit or a social network are often resized: in that case, the comparison is impossible.
